stem: Which description best fits an ontology?

options.a: A data lake that stores all of the company's raw operational data
options.b: A dashboard showing the plant's main operational KPIs in real time
options.c: A formal model of the business: things, relations, rules, allowed actions
options.d: A hierarchy of product categories and sub-categories used for reporting purposes

explanation: A category hierarchy is a taxonomy, and a lake stores what happened. The ontology captures meaning: what exists, how it connects, the rules that apply and the actions permitted.
author: claude-spec

stem: Why do many ontology efforts underdeliver, according to the course?

options.a: They rely on graph databases where relational databases would have done the job
options.b: They model the facts but skip the rules experts use to judge decisions
options.c: They are built too slowly by teams inside the company
options.d: They describe each product in far too much detail

explanation: Products, machines and suppliers are the easy part. The rules your best people apply to decide what a good decision looks like carry the value, and they are rarely written down.
author: claude-spec

stem: In data.world's enterprise benchmark, what happened when the model answered through a knowledge graph rather than the raw database?

options.a: Accuracy roughly tripled
options.b: Costs doubled with no gain in accuracy
options.c: Answers came faster, with unchanged accuracy
options.d: Hallucinations disappeared completely

explanation: Correct answers rose from 16% to 54% (Sequeda et al., 2023). The test used an insurance schema, so it proves the principle rather than a manufacturing figure.
author: claude-spec

stem: A scheduler keeps placing family F2 right after F7, which requires a full purge. Where should that rule live in the model?

options.a: On machine #7 only, recorded as part of today's machine status
options.b: On each sales order that contains family F2
options.c: In the planner's personal notes, as today
options.d: On the product family and machine type, as a constraint

explanation: A constraint that holds for every instance belongs at the type level. When it is missing, the tool generates impossible plans, the floor overrides it, and trust is lost.
author: claude-spec

stem: Where do you usually find the rules that make a plant's schedule actually feasible?

options.a: In the ERP routing tables and standard rates
options.b: In the planning software vendor's documentation
options.c: In experienced planners' heads and spreadsheets
options.d: In the plant's quality manual and procedures

explanation: Feasibility rules often live as shadow algorithms kept by experts. Extracting and encoding them, by sitting with the people and walking real cases, is core ontology work.
author: claude-spec

stem: In the course's terms, what is a knowledge graph?

options.a: The ontology filled with the company's actual facts, as nodes and links
options.b: A catalog listing every dataset the company stores, with its owner and location
options.c: A chart showing how the company's departments report to each other
options.d: A search engine that indexes all the documents on the intranet

explanation: The ontology is the model of what exists and how it relates; the knowledge graph is that model populated with real products, machines and orders. A data catalog only lists where data sits.
author: claude

stem: Your CIO says the new data lake makes the company AI-ready. What does the course say is still missing?

options.a: More storage, so that ten years of plant history fit in the lake
options.b: A model of what the data means: things, relations and rules
options.c: A faster network link between the plants and the cloud provider
options.d: A dashboard layer so managers can browse the lake themselves

explanation: A lake stores what happened. It does not say what things are, how they connect or which rules apply, which is what the ontology adds and what AI needs to act correctly.
author: claude

stem: Models get more capable every year. Does that remove the need to model your business?

options.a: Yes: the next model generation will infer your rules from your raw data alone
options.b: Yes, once the model has been fine-tuned on public industry documents
options.c: No: a model cannot know your plants' rules unless you give them to it
options.d: No, but only because today's models are still too slow for plant use

explanation: Your products, constraints and expert rules exist nowhere in public training data. However capable the model, it acts well only on the context your ontology gives it.
author: claude

stem: Your first AI use case built a model of products, machines and constraints. Why should the next use cases cost less?

options.a: The AI vendor usually discounts follow-on projects for loyal clients
options.b: The team can skip the work with experts on later projects
options.c: AI models get cheaper every year, so any later project costs less
options.d: They reuse the objects and rules already modeled

explanation: The ontology compounds: each new use case builds on what is already modeled, so the second and third need less discovery and less build than the first.
author: claude

stem: Your company switches to a different AI model vendor. What happens to a well-built ontology?

options.a: It stays, and the new model works on top of it
options.b: It must be rebuilt from scratch in the new vendor's own format
options.c: It is lost, since it lived inside the old model's training
options.d: It becomes obsolete, as newer models model the business themselves

explanation: The model is rented; the ontology is yours. It sits outside any model and stays independent of the vendor, which is why it is the asset worth building.
author: claude

stem: Which of these belongs to the rules of an ontology rather than its facts?

options.a: Line 3 has a nominal capacity of 400 units per hour
options.b: Rush orders for key accounts go ahead of stock replenishment
options.c: Product P40 is made from resin R7 and dye D2, in a fixed ratio
options.d: Supplier S12 delivers two grades of resin to the plant

explanation: Capacities, recipes and suppliers are facts. A priority between rush orders and replenishment is a rule experts use to judge a good decision, and the rules are where the value sits.
author: claude

stem: A vendor offers a ready-made ontology for your industry, set up in two weeks. What does the course say?

options.a: Buy it, since a standard industry model already covers what makes your plants different
options.b: Buy it, as long as the vendor also supplies the most capable model
options.c: Your plants' rules still have to be captured on the floor, with your experts
options.d: Decline it and wait until your data lake has been completed

explanation: An ontology cannot be bought off the shelf. What makes it valuable is how your plants actually run, which only engineers sitting with planners and quality leads can capture.
author: claude

stem: Your team proposes letting an AI model generate the ontology from the ERP tables. What will it most likely miss?

options.a: The list of machines and their codes in each plant
options.b: The products and the bills of materials recorded for each
options.c: The suppliers recorded in the ERP for each purchased material
options.d: The unwritten rules your experts use to decide

explanation: ERP tables hold facts such as machines, products and suppliers. The rules that make decisions good live in experts' heads and spreadsheets, so they cannot be generated from tables.
author: claude

stem: The same scheduling software succeeds in one group's plants and fails in another's. What best explains this?

options.a: How well each plant's own context was captured and modeled
options.b: One group bought a newer version of the same software
options.c: The failing group was running a less capable AI model behind the software
options.d: The vendor's support team favored the larger of the two groups

explanation: Context beats code. The software is the same; what differs is whether each plant's facts, constraints and expert rules were modeled before the tool was asked to decide.
author: claude

stem: Why does the course cite Palantir when it discusses ontologies?

options.a: It sells the leading off-the-shelf ontology for the manufacturing sector
options.b: Its platform is built around an ontology layer on which AI acts
options.c: It showed that large models no longer need a model of the business
options.d: It trained the first large language model built for industry

explanation: Palantir is the clearest market proof of the pattern: AI acting on an ontology layer. It does not show that ontologies can be bought ready-made for your plants.
author: claude

stem: Why does the course treat the data.world knowledge graph benchmark as proof of a principle, not a plant figure?

options.a: It compared two models rather than two ways of supplying data
options.b: It measured answer speed rather than the accuracy of the answers
options.c: It was run on an insurance schema, not on manufacturing data
options.d: It tested a single question against one small spreadsheet

explanation: The benchmark shows that grounding a model in a knowledge graph raises accuracy by multiples. Because the schema came from insurance, the exact gain at your plant must be measured, not assumed.
author: claude

stem: Your AI assistant often gives wrong answers about which machines can run which products. What improves accuracy most?

options.a: Asking each question several times and keeping the most common answer
options.b: Moving to whichever model currently tops the public benchmarks
options.c: Giving it direct access to the raw tables of the data lake
options.d: Grounding it in a knowledge graph of your plant

explanation: A model answers well about your plant only when it works through a structured model of it. Grounding in a knowledge graph raises accuracy by multiples; raw tables do not carry meaning.
author: claude

stem: Your IT team says the database schema already is your ontology. What is the key difference?

options.a: A schema says how data is stored; an ontology says what it means
options.b: A schema is relational, while an ontology must live in a graph database
options.c: A schema covers one system, while an ontology is several schemas merged
options.d: None that matters: ontology is simply a newer word for a schema

explanation: A schema describes storage. The ontology describes what exists, how things relate, which rules apply and which actions are allowed, whatever the storage underneath.
author: claude

stem: A CFO calls the ontology project 'IT hygiene with no business value'. What is the best response?

options.a: It reduces the number of servers and licences that IT has to run
options.b: It encodes the rules behind the decisions that move margin
options.c: It is required by regulation before the company can use AI at all
options.d: Agreed, so IT should fund it from its own budget

explanation: The ontology captures how the business decides: scheduling, formulation, release. That is where margin sits, so it is a business asset, not IT housekeeping.
author: claude

stem: Your ontology states that a planner may move an order between lines but not change its recipe. Which part of the ontology is this?

options.a: A taxonomy of order categories used for reporting
options.b: A record of past events kept in the data lake
options.c: The actions allowed, and who may take them
options.d: A field definition in the ERP database schema

explanation: An ontology goes beyond things and relations: it states which rules apply and which actions are allowed. That is what lets people and AI act on it safely.
author: claude

stem: Machine #7 is down for maintenance today. Where does that information belong in the model?

options.a: On the instance machine #7, as its current state
options.b: On the machine type, so that every similar machine shows it
options.c: In the setup matrix of that machine type
options.d: On each product family that normally runs on machine #7

explanation: Types carry capabilities and constraints that hold for every machine of that kind. Today's state, such as a breakdown, belongs to the instance.
author: claude

stem: A new press of a model the plant already runs arrives next month. What should the team add to the ontology?

options.a: A new machine type that copies all the rates and constraints of the old one
options.b: A new instance linked to the existing machine type
options.c: Nothing until the press has run for a full quarter
options.d: A new taxonomy branch for presses bought this year

explanation: The type already carries the rates, allowed families and setup rules. Adding an instance inherits them; copying them into a new type creates two versions that drift apart.
author: claude

stem: Your team wants to automate order release next month, before products and constraints are modeled. What do you advise?

options.a: Automate now and rebuild the model later from the system's logs
options.b: Automate now, but only for the night shift at first
options.c: Model what the objects are first, then automate what they do
options.d: Use a larger model so it can infer the constraints on its own

explanation: Automation acts on objects. If what a product, an order or a constraint is has not been modeled, the automation acts on guesses and its errors reach the floor.
author: claude

stem: A pilot agent that reschedules orders keeps confusing work orders with sales orders. What is the root cause?

options.a: The agent's prompt is too short to describe the plant
options.b: The model's temperature setting is set too high for this task
options.c: The ERP is too old to be used safely by agents
options.d: The objects and their relations were never modeled

explanation: An agent can only tell objects apart if the model says what each one is and how it relates to the others. Prompt tweaks do not replace modeling what things are.
author: claude

stem: An engineer argues a capable model can schedule straight from raw ERP tables, with no ontology. What will most likely go wrong?

options.a: Plans that break constraints the tables do not hold
options.b: Answers that arrive too slowly for the planners to use them in their daily work
options.c: Licence fees that run well above the agreed budget
options.d: Refusals to answer questions about scheduling

explanation: Capable models do not remove the need to model the business. Constraints that are missing from the tables are invisible to the model, so it proposes plans the floor cannot run.
author: claude

stem: Two next use cases have similar value. One needs mostly new objects; the other reuses the scheduling model. Which first?

options.a: The one with new objects, to widen the model's coverage faster
options.b: The one that reuses the scheduling model's objects
options.c: Either one, since the order of use cases does not change cost
options.d: Neither until a full enterprise ontology has been completed

explanation: The ontology is the roadmap. At similar value, the use case that reuses modeled objects costs less and arrives sooner, and each reuse makes the next one cheaper.
author: claude

stem: Each new use case at Polymex Industries comes with its vendor's own data model. What does the course warn about?

options.a: The plant will run out of database storage within a year
options.b: Vendors will refuse to work alongside one another on the same plant data
options.c: Nothing is reused, so each use case costs as much as the first
options.d: The models will be too consistent to catch each other's errors

explanation: Separate data models break the compounding effect. A shared ontology lets the second and third use cases reuse objects; vendor-specific models force the discovery work to start again.
author: claude

stem: Your project plan allocates no time to modeling before development starts. What is the main risk?

options.a: The vendor will charge more for its software licence
options.b: The model will run too slowly once in production on the plant's servers
options.c: IT will refuse to host the resulting database
options.d: Hidden rules surface during build, and the schedule slips anyway

explanation: Ontology work is discovery work. Rules and data gaps appear whether or not time was planned for them; budgeting the time up front avoids a slip that was coming anyway.
author: claude

stem: Halfway through modeling, the team finds planners use five unwritten sequencing rules. How should the manager see this?

options.a: As an expected output of discovery, to fold into the model
options.b: As scope creep, to be pushed to a later project phase
options.c: As a sign that the planners are resisting the project
options.d: As proof that the ERP has to be replaced before going further

explanation: Finding unwritten rules is the point of discovery. Those rules are where the value sits; deferring them means the tool will produce plans the floor overrides.
author: claude

stem: You are staffing the modeling workshops for a scheduling use case. Who must take part alongside the engineers?

options.a: The IT team and the ERP integrator, who know where the data is stored
options.b: The planners and quality leads who make the decisions
options.c: The vendor's consultants, working from the ERP configuration
options.d: The plant director, who sets the site's strategy

explanation: An ontology is built by hand, on the floor, by engineers sitting with planners and quality leads. The rules that matter live with them, not in the ERP or with the vendor.
author: claude

stem: Six months after go-live, a new line and three products were added and plans keep getting worse. What most likely happened?

options.a: The AI model has degraded through daily use since go-live
options.b: Operators have gradually forgotten the training they received
options.c: Nobody owns the ontology, so it no longer matches the plant
options.d: The ERP database has grown too large for the scheduler to read

explanation: Someone must own the ontology after go-live. Plants change; a model that is not kept in step decays, and the plans built on it degrade with it.
author: claude

stem: Who should own the ontology once the deployment is live?

options.a: The AI vendor, as part of its standard support contract
options.b: Nobody, since a well-built ontology stays stable once finished
options.c: The project team, until it moves on to the next site in the rollout
options.d: A named owner who updates it as the plant changes

explanation: Without a named owner the ontology decays as lines, products and rules change. A project team that leaves cannot be that owner.
author: claude

stem: A new product family is introduced at Ferralux. What should happen to the ontology?

options.a: Its owner adds the family with its constraints and setup rules
options.b: Nothing, as the model will learn the new family from incoming orders
options.c: The vendor regenerates the ontology at its next software release
options.d: Planners note the family's rules in their own spreadsheets

explanation: New families bring new constraints and setup rules. If they are not modeled, the tool plans them as if no rule applied and the floor overrides it.
author: claude

stem: An agent will move orders between lines. What makes this safe, according to the course?

options.a: A detailed prompt asking the agent to be careful
options.b: The ontology states which moves are permitted under which constraints
options.c: Letting the agent learn from its own mistakes on the floor
options.d: Running the agent only outside normal working hours

explanation: Agents act safely when the ontology states the permitted actions and their constraints. A prompt asking for care is not a rule the software can check.
author: claude

stem: Your agent proposed moving a food-grade order onto a line not certified for it. What is the right fix?

options.a: Add a sentence about food-grade orders to the agent's instructions
options.b: Retrain the model on last year's schedules from the whole plant
options.c: Encode the certification as a constraint on permitted moves
options.d: Remove the agent's access to that line by hand each week

explanation: A constraint stated in the ontology is checked on every action. A sentence in the prompt can be ignored or lost, and manual blocking does not scale.
author: claude

stem: Why does an agent need the ontology's allowed actions, and not only its facts?

options.a: Facts are often out of date, while the allowed actions stay fixed after go-live
options.b: Allowed actions make the agent's answers faster to compute
options.c: Facts are stored in the ERP, so the agent cannot read them
options.d: Facts say what is; allowed actions say what it may change

explanation: Knowing the plant is not the same as knowing what may be done in it. The permitted actions and their constraints are what bound an agent's behavior.
author: claude

stem: Your model covers products, machines and routings, yet planners still override one plan in three. What should be modeled next?

options.a: More attributes for each product, such as color and packaging
options.b: A finer breakdown of the routing steps already modeled
options.c: A full history of every machine's past breakdowns and repairs
options.d: The rules planners use to choose between feasible plans

explanation: Modeling products and machines is not enough. The judgment rules experts apply are where the value sits, and frequent overrides show they are still missing.
author: claude

stem: You need to record that the mold on line 2 was changed at 14:10. How should this be modeled?

options.a: As a timestamped event, separate from the line's state
options.b: As an attribute that is overwritten on the line record
options.c: As a new machine type created for line 2
options.d: As a direct relationship between the mold and the product

explanation: Events are things that happen at a time; states are what is true now. Keeping changes as events preserves history and lets the current state be derived and audited.
author: claude

stem: A recipe changes on 1 March, but February batches must still trace to the old version. What does the model need?

options.a: An overwrite of the recipe, with a backup file kept elsewhere
options.b: Recipe versions with valid-from and valid-to dates
options.c: A new product code issued for every change to the recipe
options.d: A free-text comment noting the date of the change

explanation: Temporal validity lets each batch link to the recipe version valid when it was made. Overwriting loses traceability; new product codes break the product's identity.
author: claude

stem: Resin use is stored in kilograms in one system and in pounds in another. What should the ontology do?

options.a: Store the bare numbers and let the model infer the unit
options.b: Keep only the system that already uses metric units
options.c: Attach a unit to each quantity and convert explicitly
options.d: Round both values to whole numbers before comparing them

explanation: Units of measure are a modeling primitive. Bare numbers invite silent errors of a factor of two; explicit units and conversions make every quantity unambiguous.
author: claude

stem: A batch can draw resin from several lots, and one lot feeds many batches. How do you model batch to lot?

options.a: A one-to-many relationship from each lot to the batches it feeds, with quantities
options.b: An attribute on the batch holding a single lot code
options.c: A hierarchy that places lots underneath their batches
options.d: A many-to-many relationship, with the quantity used on each link

explanation: Cardinality must match reality. One-to-many would lose batches that mix lots, which breaks traceability exactly when a recall needs it.
author: claude

stem: Should 'supplier' be an attribute of a material or an entity of its own?

options.a: An entity, since suppliers have their own properties and relations
options.b: An attribute, since each material record in the ERP holds exactly one supplier name
options.c: An attribute, since extra entities slow down every query
options.d: Neither, since suppliers belong only in the purchasing system

explanation: Suppliers have sites, lead times, certifications and links to many materials. Modeled as a text attribute, none of that can be queried or reasoned over.
author: claude

stem: Setup time depends on both the family leaving the machine and the family arriving. Where should it be modeled?

options.a: On the incoming family, as one average setup time
options.b: On each pair of families, in the machine type's setup matrix
options.c: On the machine instance, as the average setup time observed over the last year
options.d: On each work order, as a note written by the planner

explanation: Sequence-dependent setups are properties of the transition, held at type level. A single average per family hides exactly the sequencing choices the scheduler must make.
author: claude

stem: After go-live, which pattern most strongly points to a missing type-level constraint?

options.a: One operator overrides plans much more often than colleagues on the same shift do
options.b: Overrides spike during a single week of holiday staffing
options.c: The same kind of sequence is overridden on every similar machine
options.d: Plans are overridden only on days when a machine breaks down

explanation: A constraint missing at type level fails the same way on every instance of the type. Isolated or one-off overrides point rather to people, staffing or breakdowns.
author: claude

stem: A minimum batch size applies to every extruder of one type but was stored only on extruder E3. What will happen?

options.a: Nothing, since the scheduler generalizes the rule from extruder E3
options.b: Extruder E3 is excluded from every plan the scheduler produces
options.c: The rule reaches the other extruders through the type automatically
options.d: Plans on the other extruders break the rule and get overridden

explanation: A rule stored on one instance applies to that instance only. The other machines get infeasible plans, the floor overrides them and trust erodes.
author: claude

stem: Planners used the new scheduler for two weeks, then went back to spreadsheets. Its plans looked valid on screen. What is the likeliest cause?

options.a: Missing constraints made plans infeasible, and trust collapsed
options.b: The interface was too complex for daily use by planners
options.c: The planners had not been trained long enough on the new tool before go-live
options.d: The model's outputs varied too much between two runs

explanation: Plans that look valid but ignore real constraints get overridden on the floor, and after a few such plans planners stop trusting the tool. Predict this before go-live.
author: claude

stem: In a pre-go-live review, which check best predicts floor overrides?

options.a: Load-test the scheduler with ten times the usual order volume and check response times
options.b: Compare each type's constraints with the rules planners say they enforce
options.c: Confirm that every ERP master data field has a value
options.d: Walk the plant director through the scheduler's main screens

explanation: Overrides come from rules the floor enforces and the model lacks. Checking type-level constraints against planners' rules finds them before go-live; filled ERP fields can still be wrong.
author: claude

stem: A planner says, 'We always run light colors before dark.' What should you ask next?

options.a: How many years have you been applying that rule?
options.b: Could you write down all of your rules in a document for us?
options.c: When did you last break that rule, and why?
options.d: Would you agree to the tool enforcing that rule strictly?

explanation: Exceptions reveal the real rule and its conditions. A stated rule taken at face value becomes a hard constraint the floor will override when the exception comes up.
author: claude

stem: After go-live, which source best reveals the rules still missing from your model?

options.a: The ERP's standard routing tables and rates
options.b: The vendor's default configuration for the industry
options.c: The findings of the plant's latest annual quality audit
options.d: The log of planner overrides, with the reason for each

explanation: Studying overrides is one of the three ways to extract shadow algorithms. Each override with its reason points to a missing rule or to wrong data.
author: claude

stem: A planner keeps a spreadsheet with color-coded cells and hand-built formulas. How should the FDE treat it?

options.a: As a shadow algorithm, to decode with the planner
options.b: As a bad practice to retire on the day of go-live
options.c: As raw data to import into the new tool as it is
options.d: As personal notes that fall outside the project scope

explanation: Real decision rules often live in spreadsheets like this. Decoding the logic with its author turns it into explicit rules the model can carry.
author: claude

stem: Interviewing a quality lead about lot release, which approach best surfaces the real rules?

options.a: Ask the lead to describe the ideal release process step by step
options.b: Review ten recent lots: which were held, which released, and why
options.c: Read the quality manual first, then confirm each of its steps with the lead
options.d: Send a questionnaire to every quality technician on site

explanation: Walking recent real cases reveals the rules actually applied, exceptions included. Manuals and ideal descriptions reproduce the official process, not the one that runs.
author: claude

stem: One supplier appears as 'Supplier 12' in the ERP, 'S-012 Resins' in the QMS and 'V0042' in the WMS. What is needed?

options.a: Let the model guess at query time which records match
options.b: Rename the supplier the same way in all three systems so that the names match
options.c: An explicit mapping linking the three codes to one supplier
options.d: Keep the ERP record and delete the two other records

explanation: Identity resolution needs explicit, maintained mapping. Guessing at query time is unreliable, and renaming or deleting records in owner systems breaks what depends on them.
author: claude

stem: Why is fuzzy name matching alone risky for linking materials across systems?

options.a: It is too slow to run on more than a few thousand records
options.b: It cannot handle names that contain numbers, codes or abbreviations of grades
options.c: It can only run on top of a graph database
options.d: Similar names can hide different grades, so false links corrupt answers

explanation: Name similarity proposes candidates; it does not prove identity. Two grades of the same resin can differ by one character, so matches need explicit confirmation.
author: claude

stem: A mapping between ERP and MES material codes was complete at go-live. What keeps it correct afterward?

options.a: A routine that flags new unmapped codes and assigns someone to map them
options.b: A full rebuild of the mapping once a year, from fresh exports of both systems
options.c: A freeze on creating new materials in either system
options.d: Letting the model map new codes on its own, unreviewed

explanation: New materials keep appearing in both systems. Identity mapping must be maintained continuously, with an owner, or it decays like the rest of the model.
author: claude

stem: Answers about supplier delays double-count some suppliers. What is the likeliest cause?

options.a: The model's context window is too small to hold the full list of suppliers
options.b: Unresolved identities: one supplier sits under several codes
options.c: The delay dates are stored in the wrong time zone
options.d: The graph holds too many different types of relationship

explanation: When the same supplier appears under different codes across systems without explicit mapping, every count, total and ranking built on it is wrong.
author: claude

stem: When does a graph database earn its place over relational storage for the ontology?

options.a: Whenever the company decides it wants an ontology
options.b: Once data volumes exceed a few million rows across all the plant systems
options.c: For multi-hop questions and structure that varies across entities
options.d: When the team needs strict transactions and consistency

explanation: Graph storage helps with questions that chain many relationships and with variable structure. An ontology does not require it and can live on relational storage.
author: claude

stem: Your IT standard is a relational database. Can the ontology live there?

options.a: No, since an ontology is by definition a graph database
options.b: Yes, but only if the relationships are left out of the model
options.c: No, since relational tables cannot represent relationships
options.d: Yes; graph storage helps some queries but is not required

explanation: An ontology is a model of meaning, not a storage technology. Relational storage can hold entities and relationships; a graph database is a choice, not a precondition.
author: claude

stem: Which of these is a multi-hop question on a plant knowledge graph?

options.a: Which customers got batches made with resin from supplier S12?
options.b: What is the current status of machine #7 on line 2?
options.c: How many orders were shipped from the plant yesterday?
options.d: What is the standard unit cost of resin R7 this quarter?

explanation: The key question chains supplier, lot, batch, shipment and customer. The others read one fact from one entity, which any table answers directly.
author: claude

stem: In knowledge graph terms, what are 'machine', 'runs on' and 'maximum speed'?

options.a: An edge type, a node type and a property
options.b: A node type, an edge type and a property
options.c: A property, an edge type and a node type
options.d: A node type, a property and an edge type

explanation: Things are nodes, relationships between them are edges, and values describing a node or an edge are properties.
author: claude

stem: How should the model be validated before planners rely on it?

options.a: Check that every ERP field is mapped to an attribute in the model
options.b: Survey the planners on whether the model looks right to them
options.c: Experts check its outputs against recent real cases they know
options.d: Compare it with the vendor's reference model for the industry

explanation: Validation means experts testing the model on recent real cases. Complete field mapping and opinions about how it looks say nothing about whether its decisions hold.
author: claude

stem: An engineer edits a setup rule directly in production on a Friday afternoon. What practice was skipped?

options.a: A backup of the planners' personal spreadsheets
options.b: A retraining of the model on the latest plant data
options.c: An update to the user training material for planners
options.d: Versioning and review, as for any code change

explanation: The ontology drives decisions, so changes to it are treated like code changes: versioned, reviewed and tested before release.
author: claude

stem: Plans changed overnight after an ontology update. What lets you find which change caused it?

options.a: A versioned history of the model, with each change and its author
options.b: The chat logs of every conversation the model had with planners that week
options.c: A fresh export of the ERP master data from that morning
options.d: The planners' memory of how the old plans looked

explanation: Versioning makes every change traceable and reversible. Without it, a regression in plans cannot be tied to the change that caused it.
author: claude

stem: Before releasing a new setup constraint, which test plays the role of a regression test?

options.a: Ask the planner who proposed the constraint to approve it
options.b: Rerun recent real plans and check none turns infeasible
options.c: Check that the constraint parses without a syntax error
options.d: Test the constraint on a synthetic week of random orders

explanation: A new constraint can break plans that were fine. Replaying recent real cases shows its side effects; the proposer's approval and synthetic data do not.
author: claude

stem: ERP standard rates are wrong for two machines. What should the FDE do?

options.a: Override them in the ontology with the right values and leave the ERP as it is
options.b: Ask the model to estimate the rates from production history
options.c: Have them corrected in the ERP and keep reading them from there
options.d: Keep a corrected copy in a shared spreadsheet for planners

explanation: The ontology references each fact's owner system; it does not become a second source of truth. Fixing the value at the source keeps every consumer consistent.
author: claude

stem: A team proposes copying all ERP and MES data into a graph database to build the ontology. What is the main objection?

options.a: Graph databases cannot hold data coming from an ERP
options.b: Copying data is slower than asking planners for it
options.c: An ontology should hold rules only and leave the facts out
options.d: It creates a second source of truth instead of referencing owner systems

explanation: Each fact keeps one owner system. The ontology models meaning and references the owner of each fact; a full copy drifts from the source and competes with it.
author: claude

stem: Two reports show different stock for one material. Your ontology links to both systems. What must it state?

options.a: Which system owns stock for that material
options.b: The average of the two values, refreshed every hour
options.c: Whichever of the two values is the most recent one
options.d: The two values side by side, leaving users to pick one

explanation: The ontology records the owner system of each fact. Averaging or picking the latest value hides the conflict instead of resolving where the truth lives.
author: claude

stem: Your event reader turns a customer email into a quantity change. How should the ontology record that change against the order?

options.a: Overwrite the order's quantity so the order shows only the new value
options.b: As a timestamped event linked to the order, which then updates its state
options.c: As a new order that replaces the old one, under a fresh order number from the ERP
options.d: As a free-text comment on the order for the planner to read later

explanation: Events and states are separate primitives: a dated event linked to the order keeps the history, lets the fast solver react and lets you count the loops. Overwriting the field destroys that evidence.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture
author: claude

stem: A customer's audit qualifies a line for its products until the end of June. What does the qualification need in the model?

options.a: A reminder in the customer file to check the audit before July
options.b: Nothing, since the planner removes the line when the audit lapses
options.c: A flag on the line that marks it as audited for every customer it might ever serve
options.d: A validity period on the qualification, checked against each order's run date

explanation: Temporal validity is a modeling primitive: a qualification holds between two dates and the engine checks it for every plan. A reminder or a planner's memory lapses silently.
author: claude

stem: Large orders are sometimes split across two lines, but your model links each order to exactly one line. What happens?

options.a: Split orders cannot be planned or traced, so they get handled off the system
options.b: The solver runs slower, because it has fewer line choices to explore for each order
options.c: Nothing, since the planner can enter each half as a separate order
options.d: Changeover times get counted twice for every order in the plant

explanation: Cardinality is part of the model: if an order can run on several lines, the link must allow one to many. A model that forbids real cases pushes them off the system, where shadow processes start. Fake half-orders corrupt the order count.
author: claude

stem: Run rates arrive in tonnes per hour from the MES and in kilograms per minute from a line's data sheet. Plans are off by a large factor. What was missing?

options.a: A larger model that can infer the right unit from the context
options.b: A rule telling planners to check every run rate by hand at the start of each week
options.c: A unit of measure on each quantity, with explicit conversion in code
options.d: A single rate averaged across both sources every night

explanation: Units of measure are a modeling primitive: each quantity carries its unit and code converts it once. Guessing or averaging hides the error instead of removing it.
author: claude

stem: The long solver's plan beats the planner's Friday plan by 30% on changeover hours. Before anyone celebrates, what do you check first?

options.a: Whether the solver runs fast enough to be used every morning
options.b: Whether the scorecard target can be raised to match the new gap
options.c: Whether the gap comes from rules the engine does not hold yet
options.d: Whether the planner's own plan was keyed into the app correctly

explanation: A plan far better than the expert's often breaks constraints nobody encoded. A gap made of missing rules is not entitlement; walk it with the planner before it reaches the scorecard.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop
author: claude

stem: Your rule inventory has no rule on the dryer shared by two lines. The floor never starts that grade on both lines at once. What do you predict at go-live?

options.a: Plans that start the grade on both lines together, which the floor refuses
options.b: Lower run rates on both lines whenever that grade is planned on either of them
options.c: A slower solver, since it must explore many more sequences
options.d: No visible effect, since operators already know the rule well

explanation: A shared resource is a constraint across instances. Without it the solver starts both lines, the floor overrides, and trust falls. Predict such failures from gaps in the inventory before go-live.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture
author: claude

stem: Changeovers from black on one line take 150 minutes instead of 60, because that line's screw is worn. Where should this rule sit?

options.a: On the machine type, so every extruder of that model inherits it
options.b: On the product family, since black is hard to purge from any line in the plant
options.c: In the ERP routing, as the new standard changeover for all lines
options.d: On that line's instance, owned by maintenance, until the screw is replaced

explanation: The wear is a fact about one machine, not its type, so the rule belongs to the instance, with an owner who can end it. Put on the type, it would slow every similar line.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop
author: claude

stem: The procedure says the weekly plan is frozen, yet the change log shows the plan changing every day. Where do you look for the rules the plant runs on?

options.a: In the procedure, updated with a note on the current exceptions
options.b: In the people who change the plan, their notebooks and the change log
options.c: In the ERP configuration, since it records every published plan
options.d: In a standard rule library for the industry, supplied by a planning software vendor

explanation: The procedure is a hypothesis; the change log is the evidence. The real rules are run by the people who change the plan and sit in their notebooks, whiteboards and workbooks.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture
author: claude

stem: Asked why she moved an order off a line, the planner says, 'The customer would send it back.' What do you do with that answer?

options.a: Keep asking why, since a consequence is not yet a fact about the plant
options.b: Record a rule that this customer's orders go to a different line
options.c: Mark it as a personal preference and keep the system's plan as is
options.d: Ask her whether the customer's audit is the reason, to save her time in the interview

explanation: 'They would send it back' is a consequence. Ask why until the answer is a fact about the plant that holds next week and has an owner, such as a line qualification. Suggesting the audit leads the witness.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop
author: claude

stem: A planner moved an order because the customer's buyer called the plant manager this week. How should this disagreement close?

options.a: As a new permanent priority rule for that customer
options.b: As a data fix to the customer's promise date in the ERP
options.c: As not a rule: a one-off decision, recorded with its reason
options.d: As a proposed rule, left in the register until someone objects

explanation: A call this week is true this week. Turned into a permanent rule, it makes every following week wrong; closing it as not a rule, with the reason logged, keeps the model clean.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop
author: claude

stem: At a sock manufacturer, the knitting settings that work live only in senior operators' heads. What should your kickoff plan to capture them?

options.a: A survey asking each operator to list the settings they use
options.b: Walks through recent runs with the operators, who sign the rules as authors
options.c: A model trained on machine logs that infers the settings without them
options.d: A request that the supervisor write a full settings manual by the end of month one

explanation: Make the expert the author: walk recent real runs with the people who hold the settings, ask for the exceptions, and record each rule under their name. Logs alone miss why a setting was chosen.
author: claude

stem: A 2021 notebook says three changeovers per shift at most; the planner says four since last year. What goes into the rule register?

options.a: The two values, with the solver using the stricter one each time
options.b: The notebook's value, since a written source beats a spoken one
options.c: The planner's value alone, with no source needed, since she is the expert on the plant
options.d: Four as active, citing both sources, with three retired and an owner named

explanation: When sources disagree, the owner decides what holds now. The current value goes in with its sources; the superseded one is retired, not deleted, so the history stays readable.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop
author: claude

stem: Overnight, a model drafted 40 rules from scanned planner notebooks. How should they enter the rules engine?

options.a: Directly as active rules, since they come from the plant's own notes
options.b: As a block of instructions added to the event reader's prompt
options.c: Only after the IT team has checked their syntax and parameters
options.d: As proposed rules with their sources, until each owner validates

explanation: The model drafts, the expert validates, the engine applies. A drafted rule changes nothing until its owner signs it: notebooks can be outdated, and syntax checks say nothing about the plant.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture
author: claude

stem: The planner validates a new forbidden transition and it becomes active. What should be added to the code base at the same time?

options.a: A comment in the solver code that explains the rule's purpose
options.b: A test case that fails if any plan breaks that rule
options.c: A new prompt section telling the model that the rule exists
options.d: A dashboard tile counting how often the rule is applied

explanation: An active rule is tested, one case per rule in the suite, so a later change that breaks it fails before it reaches the floor. That is treating the model like code.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop
author: claude

stem: A customer that had top priority has moved to a competitor. What happens to its priority rule?

options.a: It is retired with a reason; it stops applying and its history stays
options.b: It is deleted from the register so that no future or past plan can cite it again
options.c: It stays active, since the customer might come back next year
options.d: Its weight is set to zero so the solver quietly ignores it

explanation: Retired means the rule stops and its history stays, so past plans that cited it remain explainable. Deleting it, or zeroing it without a status change, breaks the audit trail.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop
author: claude

stem: Your rules are encoded and the solvers run. How do you show the planner the model is right about her plant before she relies on it?

options.a: Show her the number of rules encoded and the solver's run time
options.b: Ask her to read the full rule register and sign every page
options.c: Run it beside her on real weeks and review every difference with her
options.d: Compare its plans with the ERP's standard lead times for each product

explanation: Validate with the expert against recent real cases: in shadow mode the system plans next to her, and each difference is a missing rule, a wrong one or a real gain. Signing pages tests nothing.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop
author: claude

stem: Overnight, a changeover parameter changed and Monday's plan moved six orders. Nobody can say who changed it or why. What practice was missing?

options.a: Versioned rule changes, each with an author, a review and an audit line
options.b: A faster solver, so the whole plan can be recomputed and checked before the shift starts
options.c: A prompt instructing the model never to alter changeover values
options.d: A weekly export of the rule register to a shared spreadsheet

explanation: Changes to the model are treated like code changes: versioned, reviewed and logged with their author, so a moved plan traces back to the change that moved it.
author: claude

stem: The ERP holds the orders; the planner holds the changeover rules. A colleague proposes copying both into a new database for the app. What do you propose instead?

options.a: Copy both, and let the app's database win any disagreement
options.b: Move the rules into the ERP so that one system holds everything
options.c: Keep the copies, and reconcile them by hand each Friday
options.d: Reference each fact in its owner system; capture only what none holds

explanation: The ontology says which system owns each fact and points to it. A new database nobody owns becomes a second source of truth; capture apps exist only for facts no system holds.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture
author: claude

stem: Why the night shift swapped an order is recorded only as free text in the line log. What does your architecture add?

options.a: A model that reads the free text and rewrites the plan on its own
options.b: A request to the MES vendor to add a structured reason field
options.c: A small capture app where the shift leader records what ran and why
options.d: A rule that every swap must first be approved by the planner

explanation: A fact no system holds is captured at the source, by a mini-app for the person who knows it, and becomes an owned fact like any other. Guessing from free text or waiting on a vendor leaves the gap open.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop
author: claude

stem: A planner asks the assistant why an order moved to Friday. Where should the facts in its answer come from?

options.a: From the model's own reasoning about the plant's likely constraints
options.b: From the solver's diff and the ids of the rules it applied
options.c: From the most similar past answers kept in the chat history
options.d: From the procedure that describes how the weekly plan is built

explanation: Code owns the facts; the model explains. The explainer turns the solver's diff and the cited rule ids into words; without them it writes something fluent that may be invented.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture
author: claude

stem: An engineer wants to paste the plant's 100 rules into the system prompt and let the model sequence the orders. What is the main objection?

options.a: The prompt would cost too many tokens on each call to be affordable
options.b: Nobody can audit those rules, and a language model is a poor sequencer
options.c: The model would first need to be fine-tuned on all of the rules
options.d: The rules change too rarely to be worth giving to a model at all

explanation: Known rules go to a rules engine, each with an id, source, owner and status; combinations go to a solver. Nobody can audit a prompt with a hundred rules, and the model cannot prove a sequence feasible.
author: claude

stem: Your event reader extracts planning events from customer emails. How should the ontology shape what it outputs?

options.a: It fills the fields of an event type already defined in the ontology
options.b: It writes a short summary that the planner reads before acting
options.c: It creates a new object type when an email mentions something unknown
options.d: It copies the full email into the order record for later search

explanation: The ontology is the model's vocabulary: it extracts into fields that already exist, which code can check (the order exists, the product exists). Prose or invented types cannot be checked or acted on.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture
author: claude

stem: The solver rejects a new order because its product belongs to no family. What does this tell you?

options.a: The solver is too strict and should skip the family check for new products
options.b: The model should guess the family from the product name each time
options.c: The order should be planned by hand from now on, outside the system
options.d: Code relies on the ontology as types; the missing link is a data fix

explanation: Code uses the ontology as types: without a family, a product's changeovers are unknown. The gap is a data fix for whoever owns product master data, not a check to relax or a guess.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture
author: claude

stem: Group IT standardizes on relational databases and objects to a graph database for the ontology. What do you answer?

options.a: A graph database is required, since relational tables cannot hold relationships
options.b: Then the ontology must stay in documents rather than in a database
options.c: It can live on relational tables; a graph helps mainly with multi-hop queries
options.d: Relational storage works only if every rule is moved into the ERP

explanation: An ontology is a model of meaning, not a storage choice. A graph database helps with multi-hop questions and varying structure, but nodes, edges and properties map onto relational tables.
author: claude

stem: Lyon's system is live. At a second plant, the ontology core fits, but planners there decide differently. Where do you start?

options.a: Load Lyon's rules and fix the differences as overrides appear
options.b: Ask group IT for the plant's ERP routings and build from them
options.c: Redo the true process walk there, with that plant's own people
options.d: Send Lyon's planner to train the local team on her rules

explanation: What worked at one site is a hypothesis at the next: local rules live in local heads, so redo the stated versus true process walk. Loading another site's rules first makes the local planner a corrector, not an author.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales
author: claude

stem: A third plant keeps its production records on paper. Taking the planning system there, what do you rebuild?

options.a: The ontology core, since a paper plant needs a simpler model
options.b: Data capture and connectors, feeding the same ontology core
options.c: The solvers, since paper plants plan with different methods
options.d: Nothing, since planners can key Lyon's export format by hand

explanation: Reuse the core, rebuild the edge: connectors are edge, so a paper plant gets capture at the source feeding objects the core already defines. Rebuilding the core or the solvers throws away the reuse.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales
author: claude

stem: You leave a plant in two months. Who must be able to read and change its ontology by then?

options.a: Site IT and the business owner, trained on it before you leave
options.b: The platform vendor's support team, under a maintenance contract
options.c: The FDE team, through remote access after the engagement ends
options.d: The group data office, which owns every model in the company

explanation: Someone must own the ontology after go-live or it decays as the plant changes. Site IT is trained on it so it can read it, change it and own it; you leave, they stay.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales
author: claude

stem: After planning, the plant wants an assistant for quality holds. What from your planning work does it reuse most directly?

options.a: The long solver's objective function and its priority weights
options.b: The planner's override log from the first months of the project
options.c: The event reader's prompt, adapted to quality messages
options.d: The objects already modeled: orders, products, lines, lots, rules

explanation: Use cases share one model of the operation: a quality hold breaks the plan, so the second use case reuses objects and links already modeled. That is why it costs much less than the first.
author: claude

stem: A customer has different codes in the ERP, the carrier file and the claims database. Your audited-lines rule misses some of its orders. What is needed?

options.a: An explicit, owned mapping from each system's code to one customer
options.b: A fuzzy match on names, rerun each time the rules engine runs
options.c: A model that guesses the customer from each order's text
options.d: A rule asking planners to check customer names by hand

explanation: The same customer under several codes needs an explicit, owned mapping; otherwise a rule keyed on one code misses orders filed under the others. Fuzzy matching can silently link different entities.
author: claude

stem: A second plant splits into two local codes what Lyon calls one product family. What do you do?

options.a: Rename the plant's codes in its ERP so that they match Lyon's
options.b: Map both local codes to the core's family, with a local owner
options.c: Build a separate ontology for that plant, starting from scratch
options.d: Keep Lyon's names and let the planners translate by hand

explanation: The ontology core is reused and local codes are the edge, mapped explicitly to core objects and owned locally. Renaming in the ERP changes another system's facts; a separate ontology loses the reuse.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales
author: claude
